ta-l3d23q1-d1e105.summary: Aquinas's divisio textus for the whole tract on the virtues in Book III, followed by the plan of Distinction 23. Having treated Christ as the one who restores us effectively, Lombard now turns to what restores us formally: the gratuitous habits that inform the soul. Aquinas maps the rest of the book. The habits themselves come first (dd. 23–36), then the precepts of the Decalogue that direct those habits to their acts (d. 37). The habits are treated singly (theological virtues, dd. 23–32; cardinal virtues, d. 33; gifts, dd. 34–35) and then in their connection (d. 36). Faith is treated in itself (d. 23), in relation to what is believed (d. 24), and in relation to believers (d. 25). He then divides the present distinction around Lombard's two definitions of faith (Augustine's 'virtue by which what is not seen is believed' and the Pauline 'substance of things hoped for'), with their expositions and attendant doubts. The paragraph closes by announcing the three questions of the distinction (virtue in general, faith in common, and formed and unformed faith) and the five articles of the first: the necessity of habits, how we know our habits, whether virtues are habits, the division of virtues into intellectual, moral and theological, and the number of the theological virtues.
claims: The habits of virtue are formal causes of human restoration, as Christ's work is its effective cause.
The theological virtues, cardinal virtues and gifts are treated first singly and then in their connection, and the precepts that direct them to their acts come after.
Faith is considered in itself, in relation to its objects, and in relation to those who believe.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e183.summary: First objection: the rational powers are nobler than natural powers, which produce their acts without habits; so the rational powers should not need habits either.
claims: If natural powers act without habits, the nobler rational powers should not require them.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e186.summary: Second objection: a power is ordered to its proper act per se, but habits are accidents; so a power should not be ordered to its act through a habit as intermediary.
claims: What is ordered per se to its act cannot depend on an accidental medium for it.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e189.summary: Third objection: nothing is easier than what lies in the will alone, and moral acts lie in the will, so no habit is needed to make them easy.
claims: Since moral acts depend on the will alone, they are already maximally easy and need no habit.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e193.summary: Fourth objection: difficulty contributes to merit, and habit removes difficulty; so habits should not be given for meritorious acts.
claims: Habits, by removing difficulty, would diminish merit.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e196.summary: Fifth objection: knowledge as a habit is just the generation of intelligible species, but species exist only in the intellect; so at least the affective part does not need habits.
claims: Habits are intelligible species and so can exist only in the intellective, not the affective, part.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e199.summary: First sed contra, from Augustine and Averroes: a habit is that by which one acts when the time comes or when one wills. This readiness is highly necessary for human beings, so we need habits.
claims: A habit is that by which one acts when one wills, and such readiness is necessary for human life.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e205.summary: Second sed contra, from Aristotle's Ethics: good action requires delight in the act, since no one is just who does not rejoice in just deeds, and delight in the act is the sign of a habit. Hence habits are needed.
claims: Delight in acting well is required for virtue and is produced by habit.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e208.summary: Third sed contra: human goodness lies in good operation, yet no one can act all the time, and goodness merely in potency is goodness only secundum quid. A stable principle between act and bare potency is needed, namely the habit.
claims: Since one cannot always act and bare potency is good only secundum quid, a habit is needed for a person to be good simpliciter.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e211.summary: Fourth sed contra: one must sometimes act well without premeditation, which only someone with a habit can do, as Aristotle says of the brave man.
claims: Acting well without premeditation is possible only for one who has a habit.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e215.summary: Aquinas's determination. He grounds the necessity of habits in a theory of rule and measure. Every ruled thing is good insofar as it conforms to its rule, and the first rule is divine wisdom. Powers limited by nature to one determinate act are rectified by their nature alone, so they fail only through defect of the power. The rational powers are open to many objects and modes and so are not determined to the good by nature; they must receive rectitude from their rule. Receiving it only passively, by being moved, would be a kind of violence and so difficult and painful. Rectitude must therefore be received as an inherent quality, so that the rule's rectitude becomes the form of the ruled power. Then it acts easily and with delight, as by a second nature. Imperfect, such a quality is a disposition; consummated and quasi-natural, it is a habit, which is hard to change, inclines to one thing, shows itself in delight, and is used at will like a possession. From this Aquinas sorts the powers. Natural powers, the sensory apprehensive powers, the will as naturally ordered to the last end, the agent intellect, and God, who is the first and unruled rule, need no habits. The possible intellect, indeterminate like prime matter, needs natural, acquired and infused habits. So do the will (in what nature leaves undetermined) and the irascible and concupiscible appetites, which participate in the rectitude of reason or, by infused habits, of the first measure. Bodily health is also a habit in this sense.
claims: Goodness and rectitude consist in conformity to a rule, and the first rule of all things is divine wisdom.
Powers determined to one by nature do not need habits, while the rational powers, being open to many, must be rectified by habits.
Rectitude received only passively, by being moved, is a kind of violence; perfect rectification requires rectitude to inhere as a quality, a second nature.
A habit is a consummated, quasi-natural disposition that is hard to change, inclines to one thing, and makes action easy and delightful.
God has no habit because he is the first rule, good by essence and not by participation.
The possible intellect needs natural, acquired and infused habits, and the will and sensitive appetites need habits insofar as they participate in the rectitude of reason or of the first measure.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e218.summary: Reply to the first objection: natural powers lack habits because they are already determined to one by nature. This reflects their lesser dignity, since they extend to fewer things, not a superiority over the rational powers.
claims: That natural powers need no habits is a sign of their limitation, not their nobility.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e221.summary: Reply to the second objection: a thing can be ordered per se to its proper act through an accident, provided the accident is not extraneous but follows from the thing's principles, as fire heats through its heat. The virtues are likewise conformed to natural principles.
claims: A per se ordering to act can be mediated by an accident that flows from the thing's own principles.
Virtues are conformed to natural principles and so are not extraneous accidents.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e224.summary: Reply to the third objection: though producing a moral act is within the will's power, the act also involves the lower powers, from which resistance and difficulty can arise. Habits are needed to remove that difficulty.
claims: Moral acts involve the lower powers as well as the will, and habits remove the difficulty that arises there.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e227.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: difficulty and facility can come either from the act or from the agent. Facility from the slightness of the act diminishes merit. Facility from the agent's promptness, as from greater charity or a virtuous habit, does not diminish essential merit but increases it, since acting with more love and delight is more meritorious.
claims: Facility that comes from the agent's readiness, as through charity or virtue, increases rather than diminishes merit.
Facility that comes from the slightness of the act diminishes merit.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e230.summary: Reply to the fifth objection: perfections are proportioned to what they perfect, so habits of the cognitive and affective parts need not be of one kind, just as the powers they perfect are not.
claims: Habits differ in kind according to the powers they perfect, so affective habits need not be species.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e242.summary: First objection: charity is chief among the habits, yet one who has it does not know it, since no one knows whether they are worthy of love or hatred (Ecclesiastes 9:1). So no habit can be known.
claims: Since charity, the chief habit, cannot be known by its possessor, no habit can be known.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e248.summary: Second objection: the habits of virtue are more spiritual than angels, since they make us spiritual, and we cannot know the essence of angels in this life. So we cannot know the habits of virtue.
claims: What is more spiritual than angels cannot be known in via, and the virtues are more spiritual than angels.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e251.summary: Third objection, against the answer that habits are known by being present in the soul: the habits of virtue are present by essence in the affect, not the intellect, and affect is not knowing. So they cannot be known by their presence.
claims: Habits of virtue reside in the affective part, so their presence there does not amount to their being known.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e255.summary: Fourth objection: many have virtues without knowing what virtue is, and some who lack virtues know much about them. So virtues are not known through their presence.
claims: Possessing a virtue and knowing it come apart in both directions.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e258.summary: Fifth objection, against the answer that habits are known through their likeness in the intellect: intellectual likenesses are founded on likenesses in imagination or sense, since the soul never understands without a phantasm, and habits have no such sensible likeness. So they cannot be known by likeness.
claims: Because intellectual knowledge depends on phantasms and habits have none, habits cannot be known through likenesses.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e261.summary: Sixth objection: likenesses are more spiritual than the things they are abstracted from, but what is in the intellect is not more spiritual than what is in the affect. So the intellect cannot abstract likenesses from affective habits and cannot know them at all.
claims: Abstraction requires the likeness to be more spiritual than its source, which fails for habits in the affect.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e264.summary: Sed contra from Augustine, cited in Lombard's text: whoever believes sees faith itself to be in their heart. By the same reasoning other habits can be known.
claims: One who believes perceives that faith is in their heart, and the same holds for other habits.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e267.summary: Second sed contra, from the Posterior Analytics: it is unfitting that we should have the habits of first principles and not be aware of them. The same holds for other habits.
claims: We cannot possess the habit of first principles without knowing it.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e270.summary: Third sed contra: whatever has a sign can be known, and delight arising in action is a sign of a habit (Ethics II). So habits can be known.
claims: Habits are knowable because delight in action is their sign.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e274.summary: Aquinas's determination on how habits are known. A thing is known either in what it is or in what follows from it. Knowledge of what it is divides into knowing its quiddity and knowing that it exists. The intellect grasps quiddities in three ways: by abstraction from sensibles; through proportionate causes or effects (disproportionate effects, as with God, give only 'that it is'); and, as with unseen artefacts, by working out what the end requires. It knows that a thing exists in three ways as well: by sense, by sensible causes or effects (as fire from smoke), and by an inclination it perceives in itself toward certain acts when it reflects on its own operation. Habits are known as to their quiddity by a mix of the last two ways. We know them through their acts, as causes through effects, and we know the acts by reasoning about what the object and end require, as with artefacts. Anyone who knows what a habit is can recognize it in others from fitting acts, even without having it. The possessor knows it in a further way, by reflection, perceiving their own inclination toward the act. This is why Augustine says such habits are known by their own presence. The properties of habits are known partly from their nature and partly from their acts.
claims: Habits are known as causes through their effects, namely their acts, and their acts are known by reasoning from the requirements of object and end.
Someone without a habit can know what it is and recognize it in others from their acts.
Someone who has a habit can also know it by reflection, perceiving their own inclination toward its act.
Effects disproportionate to their cause, as creatures to God, give knowledge only that the cause exists, not what it is.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e277.summary: Reply to the first objection: what charity is can be known by reason instructed by authority and faith. Whether one actually has charity cannot be known with certainty, by oneself or by others, because a charitable act requires something that makes it meritorious of eternal life, and that cannot be seen with certainty. One can only conjecture it from signs.
claims: What charity is can be known, but whether one has it cannot be known with certainty.
One can conjecture from signs that oneself or another has charity.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e280.summary: Reply to the second objection: we cannot now comprehend the essence of angels because we know them through acts of our own intellect, which are not proportioned to their far higher intellection. Our acts are proportioned to the habits from which they proceed.
claims: Habits can be known through our acts because those acts are proportioned to them, unlike angelic essences.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e283.summary: Reply to the third objection, with a theory of reflexive self-knowledge. The soul reflects on itself in two ways. First, a cognitive power can know its own nature and what is in it; only the intellect does this. It knows itself not through a species of itself but through the species of its object, and from that it knows its act, its power, the soul's essence and the other powers. Since it grasps in the object not only truth but every ratio there, including goodness, it also knows the will and its acts. Second, the soul can know that its acts exist. No organic power can reflect on its own act, but one organic power can perceive another's act, as the common sense perceives seeing. The intellect, being inorganic, knows its own act as it is informed by the object's species. It perceives the will's act through the overflow of the will's motion into the intellect, since both are rooted in one essence and move each other. In this way it can know a habit that exists in the will.
claims: The intellect knows itself through the species of its object, from which it knows its act, power and essence.
Because the intellect grasps the ratio of good in its object, it knows the will and its acts through the same species.
No power that uses a bodily organ can reflect on its own act, though one can perceive another's.
The intellect perceives acts and habits of the will through the overflow of the will's motion into it, since both are rooted in the one essence of the soul.
concepts: mutual motion of intellect and will

ta-l3d23q1-d1e286.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: those who lack a virtue still have principles from which they can know what virtue is and recognize it in others who act as the virtuous act. But they cannot know it in themselves.
claims: People without a virtue can know its nature and recognize it in others from their acts.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e289.summary: Reply to the fifth objection: all the intellect's knowledge of what is in the soul rests on its knowing its object, which has a corresponding phantasm. Knowledge need not stop at phantasms; it must only arise from them and, in some cases, leave an image behind.
claims: Intellectual knowledge must arise from phantasms but need not be confined to them.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e293.summary: Reply to the sixth objection: the intellect knows the will and what belongs to it not by abstracting a likeness from them but only through the likeness of its own object.
claims: The will and its habits are known through the species of the intellect's object, not through an abstracted likeness of their own.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e310.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 1 (are virtues powers rather than habits?): things have being through natural power, not habit, and every thing has a 'virtue' of being (De caelo I). So virtue is a power, not a habit.
claims: Since the 'virtue of being' is a natural power, virtue is a power.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e313.summary: Second objection: the powers of the soul stand to their acts as natural powers do to theirs, and natural powers are called virtues. So virtues are the powers themselves.
claims: Because natural powers are called virtues, the soul's powers are virtues too.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e316.summary: Third objection: 'virtus' comes from 'vis', and the powers of the soul are called vires. So the powers are virtues.
claims: The etymology of virtus from vis identifies virtues with powers.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e319.summary: Sed contra: we are praised for virtues but not for powers. One is praised not for being able to refrain from anger but for refraining in due measure.
claims: Virtue is praiseworthy and mere power is not, so they differ.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e323.summary: Second sed contra: powers come from nature and are common to all, which is not true of virtues.
claims: Powers are natural and universal, whereas virtues are not.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e332.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 2 (are virtues passions?): the mean and the extremes are of one genus, and some virtues are means in passions. So they are passions.
claims: Virtues that are means among passions belong to the genus of passion.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e335.summary: Second objection: praiseworthiness is proper to virtue, and some passions, such as shame and penitence, are praiseworthy. So some passions are virtues.
claims: Praiseworthy passions such as shame are virtues.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e338.summary: Third objection: contraries are in the same genus, and some passions, such as first motions, are sins. So some passions are virtues.
claims: Since some passions are sins, some passions must be virtues.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e341.summary: Sed contra: virtue requires the voluntary, whose principle is in us, but the principle of passions is not in us. Moreover, we are called good by virtue, not by passion: one is praised not for being angry but for being rightly angry.
claims: Virtue is voluntary and makes us good, while passions are not in our power and do not make us good.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e350.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 3 (are virtues acts?): we merit only by virtues, and only by acts, since those who compete and win are crowned, not the strongest. So virtues are acts.
claims: Since merit belongs to acts and to virtues, virtues are acts.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e353.summary: Second objection: virtue is the ultimate of a power (De caelo I), and the ultimate perfection of a power is act. So virtue is an act.
claims: As the ultimate of a power, virtue must be act.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e356.summary: Third objection: Aristotle proves that powers are not virtues because we are not praised for being able to be angry or not. By the same argument we are not praised for being merely apt for this or that, so habits are not virtues either, and virtues must be acts.
claims: The argument that excludes powers from virtue also excludes habits, leaving only acts.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e359.summary: Sed contra: Aristotle says that virtue is a voluntary habit (Ethics II).
claims: Virtue is a voluntary habit.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e363.summary: Second sed contra: Augustine says God alone works the virtues in us, but we are also causes of our own acts. So virtues are not acts.
claims: Virtues are worked by God alone, whereas acts are also ours, so virtues are not acts.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e373.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 1. By its first imposition 'virtus' suggests violence, as in a motion 'by virtue', that is, by force. Because only a perfect power can do violence, the word came to mean any perfect power, whether for subsisting or for acting. Hence virtue is 'the ultimate of a power', measured by the most it can do. Since evil in action comes from a defect of power, perfect power requires good action in its kind. So virtue makes its possessor and their work good, and it is a disposition of the perfect to the best. Human virtue perfects the human powers, those rational by essence or by participation, for good and best action. Those powers are not determined to good by their nature and are perfectly determined only by habits. So human virtues are habits, not powers.
claims: 'Virtus' first meant force and was extended to mean any perfect power, whether for being or for acting.
Virtue is the ultimate of a power and makes its possessor and their work good.
Human powers are rational by essence or by participation and are determined to the good only by habits.
Human virtues are therefore habits, not powers.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e376.summary: Reply to the first objection: the natural power by which a thing exists is determined to one thing, being, so its perfection can come from the nature of the power, and the power itself is called a virtue. The same holds for other natural powers, but not for rational powers, which extend to many things.
claims: Natural powers determined to one can be called virtues in themselves, but rational powers cannot.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e379.summary: Reply to the second objection: it is answered by what was just said about natural powers.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e382.summary: Reply to the third objection: 'vis' covers every principle of operation that is perfect, which the name 'virtus' implies. So the powers of the soul are better called vires than virtutes, especially those exercised through bodily organs.
claims: The soul's powers are more properly vires than virtutes.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e391.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 2: the notion of passion is contrary to the notion of virtue. Virtue implies the perfection of a power, while passion arises when the patient is overcome by the agent and drawn to its terms. A perfect power does not let itself be drawn except as befits it. So virtue restrains the power from being carried off immoderately by passions. Virtue is not a passion but what orders the passions.
claims: Passion consists in a patient's being overcome by an agent, which is opposed to the perfection of power that virtue implies.
Virtue is not a passion but what orders the passions.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e394.summary: Reply to the first objection: virtue is a mean in passions actively, by bringing them to the mean. So it need not be in the genus of passion.
claims: Virtue is the mean of passions as what produces it, not as a member of their genus.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e397.summary: Reply to the second objection: praise is due not only to what has the full notion of virtue but also to what shares in it, such as ordered acts that precede virtue. Passions like shame and mercy are praised because they follow from a good will that avoids the base and treats others' ills as its own. Good will is among the requirements of virtue.
claims: Passions such as shame and mercy are praiseworthy by participation, insofar as they follow from a good will, without being virtues.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e400.summary: Reply to the third objection: sin implies a defect in the operating power, so a passion can more easily be a sin than a virtue. Yet passion cannot have the full notion of sin, since it does not proceed from choice. So first motions are not mortal sins, which are directly opposed to virtues, but venial sins, and they are sins as acts, not as habits.
claims: Passions can be sinful more readily than virtuous, but lacking choice they are not mortal sins.
First motions are venial sins as acts, not habits.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e409.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 3: virtue properly implies a relation to something of which it is the principle, such as running or being. An act, being ultimate, is not ordered to anything further as to an effect. So an act cannot be called a virtue except in the way habits are named from their acts, as causes from effects. Aquinas refers to his fuller treatment in Book II, d. 27.
claims: Virtue is a principle ordered to a further act, while an act is ultimate and so is not properly a virtue.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e412.summary: Reply to the first objection: we merit by both habits and acts. Acts are the instruments of merit, since merits are essentially acts, and habits are its principles. In this sense we are said to merit by virtues.
claims: Acts are the instruments of merit and habits its principles.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e415.summary: Reply to the second objection: virtue is the ultimate of a power within the same genus, that of principle. Act is an ultimate outside that genus. So act need not be virtue.
claims: Virtue is the ultimate within the genus of principle, while act is an ultimate outside it.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e418.summary: Reply to the third objection: habits are determined to praiseworthy acts, while powers are open to contraries. So the argument against powers does not carry over to habits.
claims: Habits are determined to praiseworthy acts, unlike powers, which extend to contraries.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e437.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 1 (can intellectual habits be called virtues?): virtue is a voluntary habit concerned with pleasures and pains (Ethics II), which does not fit intellectual habits.
claims: The Aristotelian definition of virtue excludes intellectual habits.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e440.summary: Second objection: Aristotle divides knowledge against virtue as distinct, non-subalternate genera, neither of which is predicated of the other. So knowledge and other cognitive habits are not virtues.
claims: Since scientia and virtue are coordinate genera, scientia is not a virtue.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e443.summary: Third objection: virtue is defined by its order to the good, but cognitive and especially speculative habits are ordered to the true. So they are not virtues.
claims: Speculative habits aim at truth, not goodness, and so are not virtues.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e446.summary: Fourth objection: virtues are ordered to operation, while intellectual habits are ordered to knowing. So they are not virtues.
claims: Virtues concern operation, whereas intellectual habits concern cognition.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e450.summary: Sed contra: the contemplative life is nobler than the active. If moral habits that perfect the active life are virtues, the intellectual habits that perfect the contemplative life are all the more virtues.
claims: Habits that perfect the nobler contemplative life deserve the name of virtue even more than moral habits.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e453.summary: Second sed contra: according to Ethics VI, temperance, fortitude and the like are properly virtues only as they involve the intellect. What makes something so is more so itself, so intellectual habits should be called virtues.
claims: Since moral virtues are virtues through their intellectual component, intellectual habits are virtues even more.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e462.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 2 (are moral virtues distinct from intellectual ones?): 'moral' comes from mos, which is close to custom, and custom produces facility in both acting and thinking. So moral and intellectual virtues should not be distinguished.
claims: Because custom yields facility in both action and thought, 'moral' applies to intellectual virtues as well.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e465.summary: Second objection: moral science covers only what is moral, yet Aristotle treats intellectual virtues in Ethics VI. So they are moral.
claims: Inclusion in ethics shows that intellectual virtues are moral.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e468.summary: Third objection: prudence is counted among the intellectual virtues and also among the moral, as one of the four cardinal virtues.
claims: Prudence is both intellectual and moral, so the two classes coincide.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e471.summary: Fourth objection: every moral virtue lies in a mean fixed by right reason, which intellectual virtues rectify. So intellectual virtues are moral.
claims: Since right reason determines the moral mean, the intellectual virtues that perfect reason are moral.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e475.summary: Sed contra: Aristotle divides moral virtues against intellectual ones.
claims: Aristotle distinguishes moral from intellectual virtues.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e478.summary: Second sed contra: diverse perfectibles have diverse perfections. Intellectual virtues perfect what is rational by essence and moral virtues what is rational by participation, so they are distinct.
claims: Intellectual and moral virtues differ because they perfect the essentially rational and the participatively rational parts respectively.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e487.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 3 (should theological virtues be distinguished from both?): a power needs no added habit for what it is naturally determined to. Knowledge of God is naturally implanted in all (Damascene), as is desire for the highest good (Boethius). So we need no virtues with God as their object.
claims: Since knowledge and desire of God are natural, no special virtues with God as object are needed.
concepts: natural desire for the highest good

ta-l3d23q1-d1e490.summary: Second objection: the philosophers made happiness the end of all human acts, as we make the enjoyment of God, but posited no virtues with happiness as their object. So we need none with God as object.
claims: By parity with the philosophers' account of happiness, no virtues aimed directly at the final end are required.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e493.summary: Third objection: one habit knows both principles and what follows from them, and the end is the principle in practical matters. So the theological virtues, whose object is the end, should not be distinguished from the cardinal virtues, which direct the means.
claims: Since the end is the principle of action, the virtues concerning the end and those concerning the means should be one.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e496.summary: Fourth objection: perfections are proportioned to perfectibles, and the only powers perfectible by virtue are the rational by essence (intellectual virtue) and the rational by participation (moral virtue). So there can be no third genus of virtue.
claims: Since only two kinds of perfectible power exist, there are only two genera of virtue.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e500.summary: Sed contra: the Apostle (1 Corinthians 13) names faith, hope and charity, which are neither intellectual nor moral virtues, as a survey of the virtues listed by saints and philosophers shows. So a third genus, the theological virtues, must be posited.
claims: Faith, hope and charity fit neither the intellectual nor the moral class, so they form a third genus.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e503.summary: Second sed contra: God differs from creatures more than creatures differ from one another, and diversity among creatures already requires diverse habits. So virtues with God as object are distinct from the others.
claims: The greater distance between God and creatures requires a distinct kind of habit for God as object.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e513.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 1. Virtue is a habit that perfects a human power for a good act, and an act can be good in two ways. It is good formally and per se when its object is good under the ratio of good, which holds only for acts of the will or appetite. It is good materially when it suits the power that performs it, as in understanding rightly or seeing clearly. The will commands the acts of other powers and lends them something of its formal goodness, making them praiseworthy and meritorious. But that goodness lies outside the act's own species, as when one walks for God's sake with a limp. So 'virtue' has two senses. Broadly, it is any habit perfecting a power for an act good either materially or formally, and in this sense the speculative intellectual habits are virtues, as Aristotle uses the term in the Ethics. Strictly, and in ordinary usage, it is a habit for an act good formally as well, and in this sense only habits of the appetitive part are virtues, not the intellectual, and especially not the speculative ones.
claims: An act is formally good when its object is good under the ratio of good, which holds only for acts of the appetite; other acts are good only materially.
The will's commanding of other powers communicates formal goodness to their acts, but outside their proper species.
In the broad sense intellectual habits are virtues, and in the strict sense only habits of the appetitive part are.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e516.summary: Reply to the first objection: those words concern moral virtue, which is virtue in the second, strict sense. Aristotle uses 'virtue' the same way in Topics IV.
claims: Aristotle's definition of virtue as concerned with pleasures and pains applies to moral virtue in the strict sense.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e519.summary: Reply to the second objection: the solution is clear from what was said.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e522.summary: Reply to the third objection: truth is the material good of the intellect, since it is its end, and an end has the ratio of good.
claims: Truth is the intellect's good materially, as its end.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e526.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: considering the truth is itself an operation of the intellect, to which intellectual virtue is ordered. The habits called operative are further ordered to external operation. This is either making (factio), which passes into external matter as in the mechanical arts, or doing (actio), which remains in the agent and modifies its operations and passions, as in the moral virtues. So prudence is right reason about things to be done and art is right reason about things to be made.
claims: Contemplation of truth is itself an operation, so intellectual virtues are ordered to operation.
Operative habits concern either making, which passes into matter, or doing, which remains in the agent.
Prudence is right reason about things to be done; art is right reason about things to be made.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e535.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 2. Mos has two senses. In one it means custom, a frequency in things within our power to do or not do. From this the word came to signify voluntary or appetitive acts according to the appetite's inclination, whether that inclination is from nature, custom or infusion. Animals are said to have mores only by likeness, since they do not master their acts. Greek ethos likewise means both duration (as in 'hectic' fever) and morals (as in ethics). Acts are moral as they relate to the will. Acts elicited by the appetite (willing, choosing, desiring) are essentially moral. Acts the will commands (walking, considering) are moral only in their use. So the virtues that perfect the appetitive part are properly moral. Intellectual virtues perfect the intellect for acts perfect in the genre of cognition, not in relation to the will's command: knowledge makes one see the truth, not consider with right intention. So moral virtues are distinct from intellectual ones.
claims: 'Mos' means both custom and the inclination of appetite in voluntary acts.
Acts elicited by the appetite are essentially moral; commanded acts are moral only in their use.
Moral virtues perfect the appetitive part, while intellectual virtues perfect cognition apart from the will's command, so the two are distinct.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e538.summary: Reply to the first objection: the solution follows from the equivocation in 'mos'.
claims: The objection trades on the two senses of mos.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e541.summary: Reply to the second objection: intellectual virtues belong to ethics not as essentially moral but because their use, commanded by the will, is moral.
claims: Intellectual virtues fall under ethics because their use is commanded by the will.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e544.summary: Reply to the third objection: following the Commentator on Ethics VI, prudence is intermediate. It is essentially intellectual as a cognitive habit perfecting reason, but moral in its matter, since it directs the moral virtues as right reason about things to be done.
claims: Prudence is essentially intellectual but moral in its matter.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e548.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: the mean is determined by both intellectual and moral virtue, but differently. Prudence determines it by directing and showing, and moral virtue by executing and inclining to it, working in the manner of nature, as Cicero says. Socrates erred here in making all virtues kinds of knowledge.
claims: Prudence fixes the mean by directing, moral virtue by inclining toward it as a nature does.
Socrates erred in reducing all virtues to knowledge.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e557.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 3. Every agent that acts for an end must have an inclination toward the end and a kind of beginning of it. The end to which God has ordained human beings, the enjoyment of himself, entirely exceeds created nature, as 1 Corinthians 2:9 says. So nature alone does not give an adequate inclination toward it, and something must be added, as nature gives inclination to the connatural end. These additions are called theological virtues for three reasons. First, their object is God, since the inclination toward the end consists in operation concerning God himself. Second, their cause is God alone, who alone produces the inclination to an end not ordained through nature. Third, they are known only through divine revelation, not by natural reason, which is why the philosophers knew nothing of them.
claims: Acting for an end requires an inclination toward and an inchoation of that end.
The human final end, the enjoyment of God, exceeds the capacity of created nature, so a supernatural inclination must be added.
The virtues are called theological because God is their object, God alone causes them, and they are known only by revelation.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e563.summary: Reply to the first objection: although humans are naturally ordered to God in knowledge and love as natural participants in him, there is a participation in God above nature, and this requires knowledge and love above nature, for which the theological virtues are needed.
claims: A supernatural participation in God requires supernatural knowledge and love beyond natural knowledge and desire of God.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e566.summary: Reply to the second objection: the happiness the philosophers posited is reachable by natural powers, so the natural inclination toward it suffices and only virtues directing the means are needed. That is not the case here.
claims: Natural happiness needs no virtues inclining toward the end, while supernatural beatitude does.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e569.summary: Reply to the third objection: speculative principles are known by a natural habit (understanding) distinct from that of conclusions (science). In the affect, no natural habit precedes; the power itself is inclined to the connatural last end. For an end above nature, a gratuitous habit must precede the others, in the intellect (faith) and in the affect (hope and charity), where natural inclination does not reach.
claims: For the supernatural end, gratuitous habits must precede other habits in both intellect (faith) and affect (hope and charity).

ta-l3d23q1-d1e573.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: habits are distinguished by object as well as by subject. Moral and intellectual virtues differ by subject, while theological virtues differ from both by object, which exceeds the natural capacity of either part. Some theological virtues concern cognition, like faith, and share something with the intellectual virtues; others concern affection, like charity, and share something with the moral virtues.
claims: Moral and intellectual virtues are distinguished by subject, theological virtues by object.
Faith is akin to the intellectual virtues and charity to the moral virtues.
concepts: distinction by subject and by object

ta-l3d23q1-d1e586.summary: First objection: a theological virtue has God for its object, and fear of God has God for its object. So fear is a theological virtue.
claims: Fear of God, having God as object, is a theological virtue.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e589.summary: Second objection: wisdom concerns divine things, as knowledge concerns creatures. So wisdom is also a theological virtue.
claims: Wisdom, being about divine things, is a theological virtue.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e592.summary: Third objection: latria worships God and so has God as its object. So latria is a theological virtue.
claims: Latria has God as object and so is theological.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e596.summary: Fourth objection: faith regards God as first truth, hope as supreme liberality or majesty, and charity as supreme goodness. Since God has more attributes, there should be more theological virtues.
claims: If theological virtues correspond to divine attributes, there should be as many as there are attributes.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e599.summary: Contrary objection that there are only two: acting for an end requires only knowledge of the end (faith) and desire for it (charity).
claims: Only knowledge and desire of the end are required, so there are two theological virtues.
concepts: knowledge and desire of the end

ta-l3d23q1-d1e602.summary: Contrary objection that there is only one: only charity reaches God, and every virtue reaches its object. So only charity has God as object and is a theological virtue.
claims: Only charity attains God and so only charity is theological.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e605.summary: Sed contra that there are three: 1 Corinthians 13:13, 'now there remain faith, hope, charity, these three.'
claims: Scripture names three theological virtues.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e611.summary: Second sed contra: through the theological virtues we are conformed to the Trinity, so there should be three.
claims: Conformity to the Trinity fits three theological virtues.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e614.summary: Aquinas's determination. The theological virtues give the inclination toward the end, God. Any voluntary agent acting for an end must first have two things regarding the end: knowledge of it and the intention of reaching it. Intention in turn requires that the end be possible, since nothing moves toward the impossible, and that it be good, since intention is only of the good. Hence faith makes the end known, hope gives confidence of attaining it as possible, and charity makes the end good to the one who intends it by affecting them toward it. Without these one would never tend toward it.
claims: A voluntary agent acting for an end must first know the end and intend to reach it.
Intention requires that the end be possible and good.
Faith provides knowledge of the end, hope confidence in its possibility, and charity affective union with it as good; hence there are three theological virtues.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e618.summary: Reply to the first objection: fear does not imply movement toward God but a kind of recoil from him, as one considering his majesty draws back reverently into one's own smallness. So it is not among the prerequisites of movement toward the end.
claims: Fear is a recoil from God in reverence, not a movement toward him, so it is not a theological virtue.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e621.summary: Reply to the second objection: wisdom concerns divine things in this life through creatures, from which we know the creator. It does not concern God as he is in himself, as an end raised above nature, as faith does.
claims: Wisdom knows God through creatures, not as the supernatural end in himself, so it is not theological.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e624.summary: Reply to the third objection: latria has as its object not God but what is shown to God as his due. God is its proximate end, so it is a cardinal virtue (a part of justice), not a theological one.
claims: Latria's object is the worship due to God, God being its end, so it is a cardinal virtue.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e627.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: the theological virtues are distinguished not by the divine attributes but by what is required in one acting for an end before acting for it.
claims: The theological virtues are numbered by the prerequisites of acting for an end, not by the divine attributes.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e630.summary: Reply to the fifth objection: knowledge and love of the end are not enough for someone to begin acting for it without confidence of attaining it; otherwise they would never begin, especially when the end exceeds their nature.
claims: Confidence of attainment, which hope supplies, is needed to begin acting toward an end, especially a supernatural one.

ta-l3d23q1-d1e633.summary: Reply to the sixth objection: charity in a sense joins one to God really and so attains him really, which faith and hope do not. But that is not required for operation concerning God; it suffices that the agent be united to God as to the object of its operation, as sight is to a distant visible thing.
claims: Charity attains God really, but faith and hope also have God as object, being united to him as object of operation.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e305.summary: Arguments for and against the first quaestiuncula, whether virtues are powers. The objections argue from the 'virtue of being' of natural things, from the parallel between natural and psychic powers, and from the etymology of virtus from vis. The sed contra replies that virtues are praised while powers are not, and that powers are natural and common to all while virtues are not.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e327.summary: Arguments for and against the second quaestiuncula, whether virtues are passions. The objections argue that a mean shares the genus of its extremes, that some passions such as shame are praiseworthy, and that some passions such as first motions are sins. The sed contra replies that virtue is voluntary while passions are not in our power, and that we are called good for virtue, not for passion.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e345.summary: Arguments for and against the third quaestiuncula, whether virtues are acts. The objections argue that merit belongs to acts, that virtue as the ultimate of a power must be act, and that the argument excluding powers from virtue also excludes habits. The sed contra cites Aristotle's definition of virtue as a voluntary habit and Augustine's claim that God alone works the virtues in us.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e368.summary: Solution to the first quaestiuncula. 'Virtus' first connoted force and was extended to any perfect power for being or acting, so virtue is the ultimate of a power and makes its possessor good. Human virtue perfects the rational powers, which are determined to the good only by habits, so human virtues are habits, not powers. The replies grant that natural powers determined to one can themselves be called virtues and note that the soul's powers are more properly vires than virtutes.
claims: Human virtues are habits, not powers, because the rational powers are perfectly determined to good only by habits.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e386.summary: Solution to the second quaestiuncula. Passion means being overcome and drawn by an agent, which is opposed to the perfection of power that virtue implies, so virtue is the orderer of the passions, not a passion. The replies explain that virtue is a mean in passions actively, that passions like shame are praised only by participation in a good will, and that first motions are venial sins as acts, since they lack choice.
claims: Virtue is not a passion but orders the passions.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e404.summary: Solution to the third quaestiuncula. Virtue is a principle ordered to an act, while an act is ultimate and not a principle, so an act is called a virtue only as habits are named from acts. The replies explain that acts are the instruments of merit and habits its principles, that virtue is the ultimate of a power within the genus of principle, and that habits, unlike powers, are determined to praiseworthy acts.
claims: Virtues are habits, not acts, because virtue is a principle ordered to act.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e432.summary: Arguments for and against the first quaestiuncula, whether intellectual habits are virtues. The objections appeal to Aristotle's definition of virtue as voluntary and concerned with pleasure and pain, to the division of knowledge from virtue, to virtue's order to the good rather than the true, and to its order to operation rather than knowledge. The sed contra replies that the contemplative life is nobler than the active and that moral virtues are virtues only through their intellectual element.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e457.summary: Arguments for and against the second quaestiuncula, whether moral virtues are distinct from intellectual ones. The objections argue from the link between mos and custom, from ethics' treatment of the intellectual virtues, from prudence's double status, and from right reason's fixing of the moral mean. The sed contra cites Aristotle's division and the difference between what is rational by essence and what is rational by participation.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e482.summary: Arguments for and against the third quaestiuncula, whether the theological virtues are a third genus. The objections argue from natural knowledge and desire of God, from the philosophers' account of happiness without happiness-directed virtues, from the unity of the habit that knows principles and conclusions, and from there being only two perfectible rational parts. The sed contra cites Paul's triad of faith, hope and charity and the greater distance between God and creatures.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e508.summary: Solution to the first quaestiuncula. Acts are good formally, when their object is good as good, which holds only for appetitive acts, or materially, when they suit their power. The will's command lends other acts an external formal goodness. 'Virtue' broadly is any habit that perfects a power for a good act, so intellectual habits count. Strictly, and in common usage, it is a habit for a formally good act, which only appetitive habits are. The replies note that truth is the intellect's good as its end and that operative habits concern either making (art) or doing (prudence).
claims: Intellectual habits are virtues in a broad sense but not in the strict sense, which is reserved to habits of the appetitive part.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e530.summary: Solution to the second quaestiuncula. 'Mos' means custom and also the appetite's inclination in voluntary acts. Acts elicited by the appetite are essentially moral, while commanded acts are moral only in their use. So the virtues of the appetitive part are moral, and those of the intellect, which perfect cognition apart from the will's command, are distinct from them. The replies place prudence midway between the two (intellectual in essence, moral in matter) and distinguish its directive role in fixing the mean from the inclining role of moral virtue, against Socratic intellectualism.
claims: Moral virtues, which perfect appetite, are distinct from intellectual virtues, which perfect cognition, with prudence intermediate between them.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e552.summary: Solution to the third quaestiuncula. Acting for an end requires an inclination toward it and a beginning of it. The human end, the enjoyment of God, exceeds nature, so supernaturally added virtues must supply that inclination. They are called theological because God is their object, God alone infuses them, and they are known only by revelation. The replies distinguish natural from supernatural participation in God and natural happiness from supernatural beatitude. They explain that gratuitous habits (faith in the intellect, hope and charity in the affect) must precede the others, and that theological virtues differ from the rest by object, not subject.
claims: The theological virtues form a third genus, distinguished by their supernatural object, divine cause and revealed character.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e100.summary: The prooemium places Distinction 23 within the Book III tract on the virtues. It presents the gratuitous habits as the formal restoration of humanity, following Christ's effective restoration, and lays out the order of the treatment (theological virtues, cardinal virtues, gifts, connection of virtues, precepts). Within faith it distinguishes faith in itself (d. 23), in its objects (d. 24), and in believers (d. 25). It then announces the distinction's three questions and the five articles of the first.
claims: Book III's account of the virtues treats the gratuitous habits as the formal cause of human restoration.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e175.summary: Article 1 establishes why human beings need habits. The objections claim that the rational powers, being noble, need no habits, that habits as accidents cannot mediate a per se ordering, that moral acts are easy for the will, that habits diminish merit by removing difficulty, and that the affect can have no species. The sed contra arguments appeal to readiness, delight, the impossibility of constant action, and unpremeditated good action. Aquinas answers with a theory of rule and measure. Goodness is conformity to a rule, ultimately divine wisdom. Powers determined by nature to one need no habits, but rational powers, open to many objects, must receive rectitude from their rule. Since merely passive reception would be violent, rectitude must inhere as a quasi-natural quality, the habit, which makes right action easy and delightful. Natural powers, the sense powers, the will as regards its natural end, the agent intellect, and God need no habits. The possible intellect, the will and the sensitive appetites need natural, acquired or infused habits. The replies add that facility from virtue increases merit and that habits differ according to the powers they perfect.
claims: Rational powers are not determined to the good by nature and must be rectified by habits, through which the rule's rectitude becomes their form.
Habits make right action easy, prompt and delightful, and the facility that comes from virtue or charity increases merit.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e234.summary: Article 2 asks whether our habits can be known. The objections draw on the uncertainty of possessing charity, the spirituality of the virtues, their residence in the affect, the gap between having and knowing virtue, and the dependence of intellectual knowledge on phantasms and abstraction. Aquinas distinguishes knowing what a thing is from knowing that it exists, and lists three ways of knowing each. Habits are known, as to what and that, as causes through their effects (their acts). Acts are understood by reasoning from the requirements of object and end. The possessor also knows a habit by reflection, perceiving their own inclination to act. The replies hold that what charity is can be known, but whether one has it can only be conjectured. They also set out a theory of the intellect's self-knowledge. The intellect knows itself, its act and the will through the species of its object, and it perceives the will's acts and habits through the overflow of the will's motion into it. Knowledge must arise from phantasms but is not confined to them.
claims: Habits are known through their acts as causes through effects, and their possessors also know them by reflecting on their own inclination to act.
What charity is can be known, but whether one has it can only be conjectured from signs.
The intellect knows itself and the will through the species of its object, and it knows acts of the will through their overflow into the intellect.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e297.summary: Article 3 fixes the genus of virtue in three quaestiunculae: virtue is a habit, not a power, a passion, or an act. Aquinas traces 'virtus' from force to perfect power, the ultimate of which a power is capable. Human virtue perfects the rational powers, which only habits determine to good, so it is a habit. It is not a passion, since passion is being overcome by an agent, while virtue is the perfection that keeps a power from being carried away; virtue orders the passions. Nor is it an act, since virtue is a principle ordered to act, while act is ultimate; acts are the instruments of merit and habits its principles. The replies distinguish natural powers, which can be called virtues because they are determined to one, and treat praiseworthy passions as participating in virtue and first motions as venial sins.
claims: Virtue in the genus of quality is a habit, distinct from power, passion and act.
Virtue orders the passions rather than being one, and it is the principle of meritorious acts rather than an act itself.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e424.summary: Article 4 sets out the threefold division of virtue into intellectual, moral and theological. In a broad sense, intellectual habits are virtues because they perfect the intellect for its good act, the consideration of truth, which is good materially. Strictly, only habits of the appetitive part are virtues, since only appetitive acts are formally good. Moral virtues are distinct from intellectual ones. 'Mos' signifies appetitive inclination, so the virtues perfecting appetite are moral, while intellectual virtues perfect cognition apart from the will's command. Prudence is intellectual in essence and moral in matter, directing the mean that moral virtue executes as a nature does. Theological virtues form a third genus. Because the human end, the enjoyment of God, exceeds nature, God must add an inclination toward it. Those virtues have God as object, God alone as cause, and are known only by revelation. They differ from the others by object rather than by subject, with faith akin to the intellectual virtues and charity to the moral ones.
claims: Intellectual habits are virtues only in a broad sense; in the strict sense virtue belongs to the appetitive part.
Moral and intellectual virtues are distinguished by their subjects, the appetite and the intellect.
Theological virtues form a third genus, needed because humanity's end exceeds nature, and are distinguished by their divine object.

ta-l3d23q1-Dd1e578.summary: Article 5 argues that there are exactly three theological virtues. Objections propose more (fear, wisdom, latria, or one virtue per divine attribute), two (knowledge and desire of the end), or one (charity alone, which attains God). Aquinas derives the number from what a voluntary agent needs before acting for an end: knowledge of the end (faith), confidence that it is possible (hope), and love of it as good (charity). Fear recoils from God's majesty rather than moving toward him. Wisdom knows God through creatures, not as the supernatural end. Latria has God as end, not as object, and is a cardinal virtue. The virtues are numbered not by divine attributes but by the prerequisites of acting for an end. Hope's confidence is needed to begin pursuing a supernatural end. Charity alone attains God really, but faith and hope also have him as object.
claims: There are exactly three theological virtues, corresponding to knowledge of the end, confidence in its attainability, and love of it as good.
Fear, wisdom and latria are not theological virtues because none has God as the supernatural end as its object.
concepts: prerequisites of acting for an end

ta-l3d23q1.summary: The first question of Distinction 23 lays the general groundwork for the Book III tract on the virtues before faith is treated in particular. After a prooemium that sets the whole tract in order, Article 1 shows why habits are needed. Rational powers are not determined by nature to the good and must be rectified by their rule, ultimately divine wisdom. Rectitude received merely passively would be violent, so it must inhere as a habit, a second nature that makes right action easy and delightful. Article 2 explains how habits are known: through their acts, as causes through effects, and by their possessor through reflection on their own inclination. It adds an account of the intellect's self-knowledge and of the will, and denies that anyone can be certain of having charity. Article 3 places virtue in the genus of habit, distinct from power, passion and act. Article 4 divides virtue into intellectual (virtue in a broad sense), moral (virtue strictly, perfecting the appetite), and theological. The theological virtues are required because humanity's end, the enjoyment of God, exceeds nature, and they are distinguished by their divine object, cause and revelation. Article 5 derives exactly three theological virtues from the prerequisites of acting for an end: faith, hope and charity. Together the articles set the conceptual framework (habit, rectitude, supernatural end) for the treatment of faith that follows.
claims: Human beings need habits because the rational powers are determined to the good only by an inherent, quasi-natural rectitude received from their rule.
Habits are known through their acts and by reflection, but no one can be certain of possessing charity.
Virtue is a habit, distinct from power, passion and act.
Virtues are intellectual, moral or theological, and the theological virtues are needed because the human end exceeds nature.
There are exactly three theological virtues, faith, hope and charity, corresponding to knowledge of the end, confidence of attaining it, and love of it.
